data: This page describes v0.3.0. slides [deck.md] [flags] slides [command] [flags] deck.md
data.commands#Commands: Command What it does build writes the presentation as HTML, or as a PDF or images (see below). The default: slides deck.md is slides build deck.md expand prints the deck as plain Marp Markdown: templates expanded, kinds replaced by the directives they stand for notes prints the speaker notes kinds lists the kinds the deck can use and what they set themes lists the themes version prints the version (so does slides --version) completion prints a shell completion script: bash, zsh, fish or powershell slides --help prints the flags of a command. Flags may come before or after the deck: slides deck.md -o out.html and slides -o out.html deck.md are the same. Long flags take two dashes (--html); -o is the only short one. build writes deck.html beside deck.md unless -o says otherwise.
data.flags#Flags: Flag Commands What it does -o, --output file build, expand, notes output file; - for standard output --config file all configuration file; by default slides.yaml next to the deck, if there is one --no-config all do not read a configuration file --theme-set path all a theme CSS file, or a directory of them (repeatable) --kinds file all a YAML file of kinds (repeatable) --data file all a YAML or JSON file of template data (repeatable) --set key=value all one template value (repeatable) --no-template all do not expand Go templates --strict-yaml all parse directives as strict YAML, as plain Marpit does (Marp Core parses them loosely) --no-emoji all leave :shortcodes: and Unicode emoji as text instead of drawing them as images (after v0.3.0: Emoji) --html build allow all raw HTML; by default, Marp Core’s allowlist --lang code build the page’s lang when the deck sets none --bare build stack the slides, without the presenting script --pdf build write a PDF, one page per slide, with an outline — text and shapes as vectors (also chosen by -o file.pdf) --pdf-raster build write the PDF with each page one image of the slide, as v0.3.0 did --images png|jpeg build write one image per slide: deck.001.png, … --image png|jpeg build write the first slide as an image (also chosen by -o file.png or -o file.jpg) --pptx build write a PowerPoint file, one full-slide picture per slide with its speaker notes (also chosen by -o file.pptx); --image-scale defaults to 2 --odp build write an OpenDocument presentation, one full-slide picture per slide with its speaker notes (also chosen by -o file.odp) --jpeg-quality n build JPEG quality, 1 to 100 (default 85) --image-scale n build device pixels per CSS pixel for images and PDF (default 1); 2 gives 2560×1440 for 16:9, with text and vectors drawn at that density, not enlarged --allow-local-files build let images and PDF read local files, from under the deck’s directory only; refused by default, as with marp-cli
data.images-pdf-pptx-and-odp#Images, PDF, PPT:
-o with a .pdf, .pptx, .odp, .png or .jpg extension picks the format, as marp-cli does. Output directories are created. A PDF has one page per slide, at the slide’s size, and an outline of the slides and their headings.
Rendering is done by go-webengine and the PDF is written by go-pdfkit; the fonts the built-in themes ask for (Lato, Roboto Mono) come from go-opentype/fonts and are embedded, so no render touches the network. There is no Chrome.
--image-scale 2 renders at two device pixels per CSS pixel. Local images are refused unless --allow-local-files is given, and even then only files under the deck’s directory are read: a deck from elsewhere cannot reach ~/.ssh. Several and split backgrounds (![bg left:40%]) render as Marp’s layers do.
--pptx writes the deck with go-ooxml’s WritePresentation: each slide is one full-slide picture, with its speaker notes and the deck’s metadata. As in marp-cli, the slides are pictures, not editable text. The scale defaults to 2 and --image-scale overrides it; LibreOffice opens the result.
--odp writes the same thing as an OpenDocument presentation, through go-odf’s WritePresentation: one picture per slide, with its speaker notes.
data.planned#Planned: Not built yet: formulas as vectors in the PDF. When they arrive, they are a command or flag here.
data.slidesyaml#slides.yaml:
A configuration file next to the deck applies to it, so a folder of decks shares one:
kinds: kinds.yaml # a mapping of kinds, or file(s) holding one themes: # theme CSS files or directories - themes/ data: # template data company: Example Inc. html: false # allow all raw HTML lang: en Kinds: the deck’s own kinds: override the file’s and the command line’s. Data: the file’s and the command line’s data override the deck’s front matter, so one deck can be built with different data.
data.vector-pdf#Vector PDF:
After v0.3.0 the PDF is drawn as vectors: go-webengine paints the laid-out slide into the PDF instead of into pixels. The text is text, in the fonts the slide was laid out with, subset-embedded with a /ToUnicode map — it can be selected, searched and copied. Backgrounds, borders and gradients are paths and shadings, an image shown on many slides is embedded once, and links are clickable. The 100-slide benchmark deck is 758 KiB, against 837 KiB for marp-cli and 10 MiB for the image PDF of v0.3.0, and it is written in 0.3 s.
An element with no vector form here — under opacity < 1, with a filter or a rotation, a blurred box-shadow, a gradient whose opacity fades — is drawn as a bitmap of that element only, its text laid over it invisibly so it stays selectable. Formulas are still bitmaps. --pdf-raster writes one image per page, as v0.3.0 did.

data: Emoji are not in v0.3.0: they arrive with the release after it. Write an emoji as a shortcode or as the character itself: # Launch :rocket: 🎉 Shortcodes :smile: :+1: :heart_eyes: and Unicode 😄 👍🏽 👩‍💻 🇫🇷 1️⃣. Each becomes the Twemoji image Marp Core draws, with the markup Marp Core writes:
data.attribution#Attribution: The graphics are Twemoji, Copyright 2020 Twitter, Inc and other contributors, licensed CC-BY 4.0 and continued by the jdecked/twemoji project. A deck that shows them should credit them, for instance in a footer or on a closing slide. The shortcode table is markdown-it-emoji’s (MIT).
data.no-network#No network:
Marp Core’s src is a URL on a CDN, so a deck shown offline, printed, or turned into a PDF on a machine without a connection shows broken images. go-slides puts the SVG itself in a data: URI. The graphics (4,009 of them, Twemoji 17.0.3, Emoji 17.0) are embedded in the program from the pure-Go module go-icons/twemoji, 2 MB compressed and read only when a deck has an emoji.
The images are drawn by the HTML page, by --images/--image, by --pdf, by --pptx and by --odp alike: go-webengine rasterizes the SVG. All 4,009 graphics parse and draw under its SVG rasterizer; a test checks it.
The rule that sizes an emoji to the text (img[data-marp-twemoji], one em square, aligned with the baseline) is added to the theme as Marp Core adds it, so a theme of your own gets it too.
data.turning-it-off#Turning it off: --no-emoji (in code, slides.Config{NoEmoji: true}) leaves shortcodes and Unicode emoji as the text they were written as, which is Marp Core’s emoji: false.
data.what-is-converted#What is converted:
The rules are Marp Core’s; a test compares them with the HTML Marp Core 4.4.0 writes for a deck of every case.
:smile:, :+1:, :heart_eyes: the 1,903 names of markdown-it-emoji, in text, headings, links, tables, header and footer; not in code, URLs or an image’s alt text 😄, 👩‍💻, 🇫🇷, 1️⃣, 👍🏽 Unicode emoji, in text and in code: Marp Core rewrites the rendered code HTML ✔, ©, ™, ▶ stay text: characters whose default presentation is text are emoji only with U+FE0F (✔️); ❤ is the exception ☺︎ stays text: a U+FE0E after an emoji asks for the plain glyph 12:30:45, :not_a_name: stay as written A heading’s id and the outline use the emoji, not the shortcode’s name: # Launch :rocket: has the id launch-%F0%9F%9A%80, as in Marp.
Where go-slides differs from Marp Core, it converts more: ✌️ ☝️ ✍️ 🏋️ and a few other text-default characters that Marp Core’s emoji-regex leaves as text, and the handful of sequences Twemoji draws that Unicode does not list.

data.a-first-deck#A first deck:
Any Marp deck is one. Save this as talk.md:
--- marp: true theme: default paginate: true footer: "{{ .talk }}" data: talk: Pure Go slides topics: [Why, How, Next] --- # {{ .talk }} {{ range .topics }} --- # {{ . }} {{ end }} The front matter is Marp’s, plus data:. The body is a Go template: the range writes one slide per topic, each starting with ---, and the first slide is of the built-in kind title (no header, no footer, no page number).
data.build-it#Build it: slides talk.md # writes talk.html beside the deck slides -o slides.html talk.md # or somewhere else; -o - for standard output slides with no command is slides build. Flags may come before or after the deck. Open the HTML in a browser; the keyboard moves between slides.
data.expand-it#Expand it:
slides expand talk.md prints the same deck as plain Marp Markdown (output of main at 4ae5c49, 2026-10-18):
--- marp: true theme: default paginate: true footer: "Pure Go slides" --- # Pure Go slides --- # Why --- # How --- # Next The four slides the range generated, the footer with its value, and the title kind replaced by the spot directives it stands for. Anything that reads Marp — marp-cli, the VS Code extension — can take it from there, so nothing written with go-slides' additions is locked in.
data.export-images-pdf-pptx-and-odp#Export im: slides talk.md --pdf # one page per slide, with an outline slides talk.md --images png # talk.001.png, talk.002.png, … slides talk.md --image jpeg # the first slide only slides talk.md -o out/slides.pdf # the extension picks the format; out/ is created slides talk.md --images jpeg --jpeg-quality 90 slides talk.md --images png --image-scale 2 # 2560×1440 for 16:9 slides talk.md --pdf --allow-local-files # images from under the deck's directory slides talk.md --pptx # or -o talk.pptx: one picture per slide, with notes slides talk.md --odp # or -o talk.odp: the same, as OpenDocument No browser is involved: go-webengine renders the slides and go-pdfkit writes the PDF. Local images are refused unless --allow-local-files is given. The slides of a PPTX or ODP are pictures with the speaker notes attached, not editable text, as in marp-cli. After v0.3.0 the PDF is vectors, its text selectable (v0.3.0 wrote one image per page). See Command line.
data.install#Install:
Go 1.27.2 or later:
go install github.com/go-slides/slides/cmd/slides@latest slides is one static Go binary with no cgo: nothing else to install, no Node, no Chrome. This page describes v0.3.0.
data.next#Next: Marp compatibility: what is read the way Marp reads it. Templates and Kinds: the two additions. Command line: every command and flag.

data:
HCL is in v0.3.0 (go-slides/slides#13). Everywhere slides reads YAML, it also reads the native syntax of HCL2 — for its expressions and its functions.
Where YAML HCL front matter --- … --- ---hcl … --- configuration slides.yaml slides.hcl, looked up first kinds files --kinds kinds.yaml, kinds: kinds.yaml any file named *.hcl data files --data data.yaml or .json any file named *.hcl Directive comments () stay YAML, as in Marp, and the deck body stays a Go template.
data.a-front-matter-in-hcl#A front matter in: ---hcl theme = "gaia" paginate = true title = "Quarterly review" data = { company = "ACME" quarter = 3 } header = format("%s — Q%d", data.company, data.quarter) footer = "${upper(data.company)} · ${page()}/${total()}" date = formatdate("D MMMM YYYY", now()) kind "chapter" { extends = "section" class = ["lead", "invert"] } --- # {{ .title }} Attributes are the YAML keys under the same names: Marp’s directives (theme, paginate, header, footer, class, backgroundColor…), the metadata (title, author…), template, delims, kinds (file paths) and data, an object. kind "" { … } blocks define kinds, with the local directives and extends. Values reach the directives in the string forms YAML gives them — true is "true", a list of classes is a list — so a directive behaves the same whichever syntax set it. null leaves a directive unset. data keeps its types: in templates an integral number is an int, other numbers a float64, and lists and objects stay lists and maps, so {{ add .quarter 1 }} works. An HCL value is final: Go templates do not run over it a second time.
data.errors#Errors:
Errors are HCL’s diagnostics, positioned in the deck file itself: footer = data.compnay on the deck’s fourth line gives
deck.md:4:14: Unsupported attribute: This object does not have an attribute named "compnay".
data.functions#Functions: page(), total() the page number and the last page number, as {{ page }} and {{ total }}: a footer paginates now(), timestamp() the time, RFC 3339, local and UTC; formatdate formats it env(name) an environment variable, "" when unset file(path) a UTF-8 text file of at most 1 MiB, relative to the deck or the configuration file numbers abs ceil floor log max min parseint pow signum strings chomp format formatlist join lower regex regexall regexreplace replace split strlen strrev substr title trim trimprefix trimspace trimsuffix upper collections chunklist coalesce coalescelist compact concat contains distinct element flatten keys length lookup merge range reverse slice sort values zipmap encodings csvdecode jsondecode jsonencode dates formatdate timeadd All but the first four rows are go-cty’s standard library. None reaches the network.
data.licences#Licences: HCL support links hashicorp/hcl (MPL-2.0, used unmodified as a library) and zclconf/go-cty (MIT).
data.marp-and-slides-expand#Marp and slides e:
Marp reads ---hcl as the start of a front matter too — its front-matter rule opens on any first line that begins with three dashes — and, the block not being a YAML mapping, applies none of it: the deck still renders in Marp, without its directives. A test pins this against Marp Core’s own output.
slides expand writes the front matter back as YAML, so the expanded deck is plain Marp and renders as slides renders the original:
--- theme: "gaia" paginate: true title: "Quarterly review" header: "ACME — Q3" footer: "ACME · 1/2" date: "19 October 2026" ---
data.slideshcl#slides.hcl:
kinds = "kinds.hcl" # or a list of files themes = ["themes/acme.css"] data = { company = "ACME" } # or file paths html = false lang = "en" kind "quote" { extends = "blank" footer = "${data.company}" } An unknown attribute is an error, not a silent no-op. A kinds file holds kind blocks; its other attributes are ignored, so slides.hcl can serve as one. A data file’s attributes are the data’s keys:
# data.hcl company = "ACME" year = 2026 motto = trimspace(file("motto.txt"))
data.variables#Variables:
data is the template data: the front matter’s own data, overlaid by slides.hcl’s, by --data files and by --set. "${data.company}" works wherever {{ .company }} would.
Front-matter attributes may reference data.* but not each other: footer = title is an error. Spot directives (_class…) are not HCL identifiers; write them in a comment.

data: A kind is a named preset of local directives: header, footer, pagination, class, background. A slide says what it is — title, section — instead of repeating how it looks, and a deck’s look is changed in one place.
data.built-in#Built in: Kind Sets title class: lead, no page number, no header, no footer section class: lead content nothing: the deck’s own defaults blank no page number, no header, no footer Any of them can be redefined.
data.defining-kinds#Defining kinds:
In the front matter:
--- marp: true kinds: chapter: class: invert backgroundColor: "#1e1b4b" paginate: false quote: extends: blank class: quote --- extends starts a kind from another one’s directives. A kind accepts the local directives and extends.
data.leaving-go-slides#Leaving go-slides: slides expand writes every kind out as the spot directives it stands for, slide by slide, so the result is plain Marp Markdown that any Marp tool reads.
data.sharing-kinds#Sharing kinds:
A team’s kinds belong in one file every deck names:
# kinds.yaml chapter: class: invert paginate: false --- marp: true kinds: kinds.yaml # or a list of files --- or --kinds kinds.yaml on the command line, or kinds: in slides.yaml. The order is: the built-in kinds, then the command line and the configuration file, then the deck’s own kinds:.
slides kinds talk.md lists the kinds a deck can use and what each one sets.
data.using-a-kind#Using a kind: # Part two --- ![bg](photo.jpg) kind: applies like a local directive: to this slide and the ones after it. _kind: applies like a spot directive: to this slide only. Switching kinds first clears what the previous kind set, so a class or a footer never leaks from one kind into the next. Directives written on the slide itself win over the kind.

data: A deck written for Marp is a go-slides deck. The rules below are Marpit’s and Marp Core’s; where go-slides differs, this page says so.
data.around-the-slide#Around the slide: Header and footer: header: and footer: directives, in Markdown. Pagination: paginate: true. Speaker notes: an HTML comment that is not a directive is a note. slides notes prints them. Fragmented lists: a list written with * (or 1)) appears item by item, as in Marp.
data.directives#Directives: Kind Where Applies to global front matter, or anywhere the whole deck: theme, style, headingDivider, lang… local this slide and the ones after it spot (underscore) this slide only The local directives are Marpit’s: paginate, header, footer, class, backgroundColor, backgroundImage, backgroundPosition, backgroundRepeat, backgroundSize, color. Directives are parsed as loose YAML, as Marp Core does; --strict-yaml parses them as plain Marpit does.
data.images#Images: ![bg](image.jpg) makes an image the slide’s background, with Marp’s keywords: bg contain, bg cover, bg 50%, bg left/bg right for a split background, several bg images side by side, and the image filters (blur, sepia, grayscale…). Inline image sizes (w:200px, h:) are read as Marp reads them.
data.slides#Slides: A horizontal ruler — --- on a line of its own, as Marpit splits — starts a new slide, and so does a heading of the level the headingDivider directive names. The front matter, between the first two ---, holds global directives and the deck’s data.
data.themes#Themes: default, gaia and uncover are built in, selected with theme:. A theme of your own is a CSS file with Marp’s /* @theme name */ comment, given with --theme-set or listed under themes: in slides.yaml.
data.where-go-slides-differs#Where go-slides: Templates. {{ }} in the body is a Go template action (see Templates). A deck that shows {{ as text outside a code block needs --no-template, or the text escaped as Go templates escape it. Code blocks and code spans are left alone. Kinds. kind: and _kind: are directives Marp does not have (see Kinds). slides expand replaces them with the directives they stand for, so the expanded deck is plain Marp. Outputs. HTML, PNG, JPEG, PDF, PPTX and ODP, through Go libraries rather than a headless browser (see Command line for the known limit). As in marp-cli, a PPTX holds pictures, not editable text. Fitting headings. # Title is supported: the heading fills the slide width on one line, in the page and in every export. Math and code. $…$ and $$…$$ follow Marp Core’s delimiter rules and are typeset by go-tex/math; fenced code is highlighted by go-rouge with highlight.js class names (see Math and code).

data: Math and code are in v0.2.0.
data.code#Code:
Fenced code blocks are coloured by go-rouge, which writes highlight.js class names, the ones Marp’s themes style:
```go fmt.Println("hello") ``` A language go-rouge does not know is written as plain text, as Marp Core does.
data.fonts#Fonts: Lato Regular, Bold, Black and italics and Roboto Mono Regular, Bold and italics are embedded, so gaia’s headings get their weight and italic text renders italic.
data.math#Math:
$…$ is an inline formula and $$…$$ a display formula:
The famous one is $E=mc^2$, and this is a display formula: $$ \int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} $$ The delimiter rules are Marp Core’s, read from marp-core 4.4.0: a $ followed by a space does not open a formula, and one followed by a digit does not close it, so prices such as $5 and $10 stay text. go-tex/math typesets each formula into inline SVG sized in em, so it follows the text’s size and sits on its baseline. The same SVG is used in the HTML page, in images and in the PDF. A formula that does not parse stays visible as written; the error is kept in its title.

data:
These figures are for v0.3.0, which renders slides concurrently and parses its fonts once (go-slides/slides#11). go-slides and marp-cli 4.5.1 were run as subprocesses on the same decks, on an Apple M4 Max (16 CPUs) with a 1-minute load average under 8, five interleaved rounds after a warm-up. Time is the median wall time; memory is the peak of the whole process tree (marp-cli drives a Chrome, whose processes count).
Deck Output go-slides marp-cli go-slides memory marp-cli memory 100 slides HTML 36 ms 315 ms 47 MiB 140 MiB 100 slides PDF 1.14 s 1.88 s 242 MiB 1,509 MiB 100 slides PNG, every slide 0.97 s 5.44 s 225 MiB 1,354 MiB 100 slides PPTX 3.39 s 8.03 s 530 MiB 1,373 MiB gaia, 20 slides PDF 283 ms 1.57 s 154 MiB 1,315 MiB math and code, 20 slides PNG, every slide 250 ms 2.32 s 168 MiB 1,286 MiB
data.vector-pdf#Vector PDF:
After v0.3.0 the PDF is drawn as vectors (see Command line). Same machine and method, 2026-10-19:
Deck go-slides marp-cli v0.3.0 go-slides size marp-cli size v0.3.0 size 100 slides 306 ms 1,763 ms 1,147 ms 758 KiB 837 KiB 10.0 MiB gaia, 20 slides 93 ms 1,546 ms 285 ms 32 KiB 66 KiB 582 KiB math and code, 20 slides 140 ms 1,643 ms 294 ms 124 KiB 335 KiB 638 KiB Memory for the 100-slide PDF: 161 MiB, against 1,509 MiB for marp-cli; CPU time 0.9 s against 2.7 s.
data.what-it-does-not-win#What it does not wi: PDF size, in v0.3.0. Each slide was an image in the PDF: 10 MiB against 837 KiB for the 100-slide deck. The vector PDF above is smaller than marp-cli’s. CPU time on big decks. Four workers spend more CPU than the wall time shows: in v0.3.0, 3.2 s against marp-cli’s 2.7 s for the 100-slide PDF (0.9 s for the vector PDF). Memory is an upper bound for marp-cli: Chrome’s processes share pages that the sum counts in each. Its largest single process is 220–320 MiB. The method, every deck and mode, and the commands to reproduce the figures are in BENCHMARKS.md.
data.why-it-is-fast#Why it is fast: No browser to start. marp-cli launches Chrome for every PDF, image and PPTX export; go-slides renders with go-webengine inside its own process. Slides render in parallel, four at a time by default, and each image is written as soon as it is its turn: a long deck is never held in memory as images. Fonts are parsed once per process, not once per slide.

data: The deck is a Go text/template, evaluated before the Markdown is parsed. Everything the Go template language has — actions, pipelines, if, range, with, variables — works in a deck.
data.code-is-left-alone#Code is left alone: Fenced code blocks and inline code spans are set aside before the template runs and restored verbatim, so a slide about Go templates can show {{ .Name }} without escaping it.
data.data#Data:
The template’s dot holds the front matter’s keys, then the keys of its data: mapping, then the data given on the command line or in slides.yaml — each overriding the one before.
--- marp: true title: Quarterly review data: team: Platform --- # {{ .title }} Presented by the {{ .team }} team. From the command line:
Flag Gives --data file.yaml a YAML or JSON file of data (repeatable) --set key=value one value (repeatable)
data.generating-slides#Generating slides:
The whole body is one template, so a range that writes --- writes slides:
{{ range .releases }} --- # {{ .version }} {{ range .changes }}- {{ . }} {{ end }} {{ end }}
data.include#Include: {{ include "parts/agenda.md" }} inserts another file, relative to the deck.
data.page-and-total#Page and total: {{ page }} and {{ total }} are the slide’s number and the number of slides. They are known only once the deck has been split, so they are filled in then — a generated deck counts the slides it generated.
data.turning-it-off#Turning it off: --no-template reads the deck as plain Marp: {{ is text.
